Hey HN, I'm Shreyash from Feyn. We help companies build custom models from their data. Today we're releasing Critic, a change review platform that lets you engage directly with the AI that wrote the code.

Agents write most of our code. While that has made us more productive, understanding a change and its consequences has become incredibly difficult. As our company adopted more agentic tools, we found it harder to loop people in on the impact of a PR and the state of a project. We built Critic to fix this.

Critic lets AI agents present their code, annotate key blocks, and include relevant evidence (like screenshots and instructions to run locally). Anyone viewing that change can talk directly to the agent that wrote it. See a demo here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=U2--lytmOtQ.

Critic works through a plugin for Codex or Claude Code. When your agent writes code, the plugin asks it to also write a narrative describing the story behind the change, and highlight any assumptions, decisions, or complex code. You can then view the change at critic.run or have your agent pull it via the bundled MCP. Every feature in Critic is available over MCP, so your agent gets all the same context without leaving its harness.

From the dashboard or MCP, you can chat with the authoring agent directly. When Critic receives a question, it forks the authoring session and forwards your question there. That way your main thread stays clean and keeps working.

Local changes are visible only to the owner. Anything pushed to GitHub is mirrored and visible to anyone with permission to view that change on GitHub.

When building Critic, security was a big priority for us. AI agents often run in auto mode and can take many actions on your computer. We wanted to ensure that giving people access to your agent doesn't mean giving them access to your computer. All Critic forked sessions are stripped of their write tools. They can only answer questions about the change and in-progress work in that workspace.

Critic has helped us catch several incidents before they hit production. The most common is a model not reusing artifacts, like existing styles, components, or functions. Because it's so easy to dig into an agent's work and question it, we've also caught more cases of models misdiagnosing issues or writing unhelpful code. Since Critic's UI is faster and friendlier to agents than GitHub, our team is returning feedback quicker as well.

Critic is free to use. Sign up at https://critic.run. Let me know if you have feedback or questions.

## Why this EPIC

Synapse finds, verifies and reports security issues, but almost none of that reaches the tools where teams work. A new critical finding, a breached SLA, a pending approval, an expiring risk acceptance or a finished DAST run stays inside the console until someone opens it. There is no Jira handoff, no Confluence page, no Teams or Telegram channel, and no per-person routing.

This EPIC closes the gap end to end: event producers, delivery, message content with default and custom templates, channels, ticketing, documentation publishing, per-user routing, inbound webhooks and the admin UI.

Priority: the notification and integration flows come first. Every alert must reach chat, email, pager and ticketing with a sensible built-in template, and a tenant must be able to replace that template with its own wording without a code change.

- Code audit of `main` at `09f9a927` (2026-09-25). Every claim below cites the file that backs it.
- An architecture, security and fact-check review of the first draft. Its findings are folded into this text.

# Kingdom Network Control Room

This issue is the live coordination hub for all parallel ChatGPT workstreams on Kingdom Network.

## Source of truth
- Master roadmap: `docs/KINGDOM_NETWORK_BUILD_CHECKLIST.md`
- Repository: `BroMarcus/church-app`
- Deployment policy: HOLD all independent deployments until Marcus approves one combined deployment.
- Active work should use dedicated workstream branches rather than writing directly to `main` whenever practical.

## Required worker protocol
Before doing Kingdom Network work, every chat/workstream must:
1. Read the current repository state.
2. Read `docs/KINGDOM_NETWORK_BUILD_CHECKLIST.md`.
3. Read this Control Room issue and latest comments.
4. Check whether another workstream has already claimed the same feature, route, component, database object, RLS policy, migration, or related dependency.
5. If there is meaningful overlap, do not independently modify it. Pick another unclaimed priority or explicitly coordinate the dependency.
6. Post a `CLAIMED` update before starting significant work.
7. Work from the master checklist priority order unless Marcus gives a direct override.
8. Verify behavior before declaring completion; written code alone is not complete.
9. Post a final status as `VERIFIED`, `BLOCKED — MARCUS`, `BLOCKED — TECHNICAL`, or `READY FOR COMBINED DEPLOYMENT`.
10. If blocked on Marcus but other safe work exists, record the blocker and continue to the next unclaimed priority.
11. Do not deploy independently.
12. Do not blindly merge competing changes.
13. New product ideas must be added to the shared roadmap rather than living only inside one chat.

### CLAIMED
- Workstream/chat:
- Task:
- Routes/features:
- Files/components likely affected:
- Supabase tables/functions/RLS/migrations affected:
- Dependencies:
- Deployment: HOLD

### Completion
- Status: VERIFIED / BLOCKED — MARCUS / BLOCKED — TECHNICAL / READY FOR COMBINED DEPLOYMENT
- What changed:
- What was tested:
- Remaining risk/blocker:
- Files/database objects touched:
- Deployment: HOLD unless Marcus explicitly approves combined deployment

## Status meanings
- `CLAIMED` — actively being worked
- `DONE — NEEDS VERIFICATION` — implementation exists but has not been proven end-to-end
- `VERIFIED` — behavior has been tested and confirmed
- `BLOCKED — MARCUS` — needs a decision, approval, credential, content, or other user input
- `BLOCKED — TECHNICAL` — genuine technical blocker after reasonable alternate approaches
- `READY FOR COMBINED DEPLOYMENT` — verified and queued for integration

bug: get-analytics-overview is missing from the api:read automation catalogue

## Description

`GET /api/v1/analytics` already exists as the `get-analytics-overview` operation, but the operation is not included in the automation catalogue used to authorize workspace-scoped `api:read` tokens.

As a result, a correctly scoped read-only API token can access other allowed workspace resources but receives `403` when requesting the stored analytics endpoint.

The endpoint itself appears to be a read operation over analytics already stored by OpenPost, so this looks like an authorization-catalogue omission rather than a request for new analytics functionality.

I have also confirmed that the catalogue entry remains absent in OpenPost v6.1.3 and current `main`.

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Create or use an API token scoped to a workspace with `api:read`.
2. Confirm that the token can access an allowed workspace read endpoint, for example:

   `GET /api/v1/workspaces`

3. Request:

   `GET /api/v1/analytics`

4. Observe that the request is rejected with `403`.

5. Inspect:

   `apps/server/internal/automationcatalog/catalog.go`

   The catalogue includes workspace-scoped read operations such as `list-accounts`, but does not include `get-analytics-overview`.

A minimal catalogue entry that resolves the authorization gap is:

```go
withSelectors(read("get-analytics-overview", ExposureAlpha), workspaceSelector()),
```

I have tested this change in a downstream compatibility build. With no other authorization change, the same workspace-scoped `api:read` token changes from `403` to a successful analytics response, while write operations remain unavailable.

## Expected Behavior

A workspace-scoped `api:read` token should be able to call the existing stored-data analytics endpoint for its permitted workspace.

The authorization should remain workspace-scoped and read-only.

## Actual Behavior

`GET /api/v1/analytics` returns `403` to a valid workspace-scoped `api:read` token because `get-analytics-overview` is absent from the read automation catalogue.

## Screenshots

N/A — this is an API authorization issue.

## Environment

- OpenPost version: reproduced on v5.1.2; catalogue omission also confirmed in v6.1.3 and current `main`
- Deployment method: Docker
- Operating system: Linux
- Go version (if building from source): N/A
- Browser (if web UI issue): N/A

## Logs

```text
GET /api/v1/workspaces -> 200
GET /api/v1/analytics  -> 403
```

Sensitive token and workspace details omitted.

## Additional Context

The analytics route already exists and is registered as operation `get-analytics-overview`.

The proposed change is therefore limited to admitting that existing GET operation to the read automation catalogue with the existing workspace selector:

```go
withSelectors(read("get-analytics-overview", ExposureAlpha), workspaceSelector()),
```

This preserves the intended boundary:

- read-only access;
- workspace-scoped access;
- no publishing permission;
- no provider credential access;
- no additional provider mutation capability.

I would be happy to submit the corresponding small PR with a regression test if that would be useful.

Contract step of #6379 (expand step: PR #6993). Ship in the release **after** the one that carries #6993, so an image rollback across that release still delivers alerts.

## Why this is separate
#6993 moves notification channel `config` into `notification_channel_configs` (ownership-gated RLS) but keeps the legacy `notification_channels.config` column for one release as a write-only mirror, so the previous image, which reads only that column, keeps delivering after a rollback.

**Until this ships, the DB-layer confidentiality fix for #6379 is incomplete:** an org-scoped DB session can still read the legacy `config` column of its MSP's partner-wide channel rows through the partner-wide SELECT branch. The application never reads that column (guarded by `notificationChannelLegacyConfig.test.ts`) and API responses are still redacted, so this is a defence-in-depth gap, not a known exploitable path.

## Work
1. New migration (sorted after the newest on main):
   - Resync first: `INSERT INTO notification_channel_configs (channel_id, config) SELECT id, config FROM notification_channels WHERE config IS NOT NULL ON CONFLICT (channel_id) DO UPDATE SET config = EXCLUDED.config` (elect `breeze.scope = system` first; report the row count). The sync trigger should keep the copies equal already, so this is belt-and-braces.
   - `DROP TRIGGER IF EXISTS notification_channels_sync_legacy_config ON notification_channels;` `DROP FUNCTION IF EXISTS public.notification_channels_sync_legacy_config();`
   - `ALTER TABLE notification_channels DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS config;`
2. `services/notificationChannelConfig.ts`: remove `legacyNotificationChannelConfigColumn` and the legacy UPDATE in `writeNotificationChannelConfig` (stop writing both).
3. Remove the `notification_channels.config` entry from `encryptedColumnRegistry.ts` and `config` from the `notification_channels` export policy (`tenantExportPolicyRegistry.ts`, `excludedOpen`).
4. Delete `notificationChannelLegacyConfig.test.ts`. Update `notificationChannelConfigsRls.integration.test.ts`: assert the column is gone (42703 for an org session) and drop the rollback-path cases. 5. Update the schema comment in `db/schema/alerts.ts`.

Escrow `deposit` accepts zero/negative/uncapped amounts and post-deadline deposits

## Context
Soroban escrow contract, `contracts/soroban/contracts/escrow/src/lib.rs:37-55`.

## Problem
`deposit` has no `amount > 0` check, no per-deposit cap, accepts deposits after `target` has been reached, and the deadline boundary uses `>=` (off by one). `platform_fee` is also never validated against the total.

## Impact
Invalid or abusive states: zero deposits, donations after funding ends, overshoot beyond target with no cap.

## Suggested solution
Validate `amount > 0`, enforce a per-deposit cap, reject deposits after the campaign is funded or past deadline (with clear boundary semantics), and validate fee amounts.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Reject zero/negative amounts
- [ ] Reject deposits after target reached or deadline passed (exact boundary)
- [ ] Enforce a per-deposit maximum
- [ ] Validate platform fee against deposit amount

Orphan sweep liveness keys on discovery.lock, which nothing in-tree writes and NEAT-AI spells .discovery.lock (src/discovery_cleanup.rs::is_directory_orphaned)

<!-- finding-id: SEC-bbe3f392d7aa -->
<!-- cwe: CWE-706 -->

The orphan sweep's only liveness signal is a file named `discovery.lock`
(`discovery_cleanup.rs::LOCK_FILE_NAME`), but **no production code in this
crate writes it**, and the one known host — NEAT-AI — writes
**`.discovery.lock`** (leading dot) into each session directory. A host that
calls the FFI `clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs` on NEAT-AI's `.discovery/`
root therefore reads every live session as orphaned and deletes it with its
in-flight data. Severity low (NEAT-AI does not bind the FFI sweep today, so no
live path), confidence high (both names verified, deletion reproduced).

Found by the chunk 11 security sweep, Issue #2234 (tracker #2095).

## Why this matters

- `discovery_cleanup.rs::is_directory_orphaned` treats a directory as
  abandoned exactly when `<dir>/discovery.lock` is absent;
  `clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs_since` then removes every such directory
  older than the scan start.
- `LOCK_FILE_NAME` has no in-tree production writer — only tests create it.
  The contract lives in the caller: `docs/FFI_API.md` § "Orphaned Directory
  Sweep" and the doc comment on `ffi/utilities.rs::clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs`
  say a subdirectory "is considered orphaned when it has no
  `discovery.lock` file".
- NEAT-AI `src/discovery/DiscoveryCleanup.ts` declares
  `const LOCK_FILE_NAME = ".discovery.lock"` and writes it from
  `createDiscoveryLockFile`. The two names never match, so the ownership
  signal the sweep relies on is unenforced: nothing in either repo checks
  that the writer and the reader agree.
- The #1903 age floor only protects directories touched *after* the scan
  starts; a long-running session whose directory was last modified earlier
  gets no protection.

Reproduced against the current tree: a `.discovery/<uuid>/` holding only
`.discovery.lock` is swept with `removed: 1` and the directory is gone.

## Attacker model

No attacker needed — this is an integrity/availability defect triggered by
ordinary host behaviour. The trigger is a host (today's NEAT-AI, or a future
refactor that adopts the Rust sweep in place of its TypeScript one) invoking
the FFI sweep on a root its own sessions populate.

## Trigger

`clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs({"baseDir": ".discovery"})` while NEAT-AI
sessions are running under `.discovery/<creature-uuid>/`.

## Exploit sketch

1. NEAT-AI starts a discovery session: `.discovery/<uuid>/` with
   `.discovery.lock` inside, data being written.
2. Any caller runs the FFI sweep on `.discovery`.
3. `is_directory_orphaned` probes `discovery.lock` → `NotFound` → orphaned;
   the directory predates the scan, so the age floor passes it; the #1903
   re-check probes the same wrong name and passes it too.
4. `fs::remove_dir_all` deletes the live session's recording.

## Suggested fix

Make the sweep fail closed on either spelling: treat a directory as in use
when `discovery.lock` **or** `.discovery.lock` is present (in
`is_directory_orphaned`, and in the `assert_is_discovery_dir` contents
check), document both in `docs/FFI_API.md`, and note the host's spelling
beside `LOCK_FILE_NAME`. The fix ships
`tests/issue_2256_orphan_sweep_host_lock_name.rs`, which **fails before the
fix**: a `.discovery/<uuid>/` holding only `.discovery.lock` must survive
`clean_orphaned_discovery_dirs` (the session directory is the canary) with
`removed == 0`.

* compare that pattern against JamesJedi420/containment-protocol#1068 competency/practice progression and current specialization-growth rules

* preserve completed JamesJedi420/containment-protocol#3282 risk-weighted standing rewards as the existing standing/fame solution rather than recreating it
* test whether risk-adjusted progression can be represented as bounded practice quality, experience weighting, learning opportunity, or another existing progression input without introducing a generic flat-stat ladder
* test exploit pressure from farming nominally high-difficulty work, repeatable trivialized assignments, party-size manipulation, or other ways difficulty labels could become a permanent-stat optimization loop
* determine whether the imported rule should be rejected, translated into existing progression semantics, or requires a genuinely missing implementation boundary

## Constraints

* contradiction-check only until disposition is approved
* no implementation child or new reward umbrella may be created from this candidate before this check closes
* no reopening completed JamesJedi420/containment-protocol#3282 standing rewards
* no parallel level, OVR, generic stat, or difficulty-progression system
* no assumption that a difficulty label itself proves greater learning value
* preserve deterministic progression and existing partial-observability rules

* JamesJedi420/containment-protocol#1068 unified skill, progression, and competency framework

* final disposition is recorded as reject, fold/update existing owner, or reconcile a new bounded implementation issue

Complete only when the candidate has one explicit CP-native disposition and the authoritative progression/difficulty owner is identified. Until then, downstream implementation remains held.

Design/reconciliation first; Codex implementation only if a bounded CP-compatible mechanic survives the check.

security: tenant scope becomes an explicit three-state value that fails closed

## Problem

Tenant authorization in the controller is expressed as a bare string, and an empty
string means "root, allow everything". `isWithinTenantScope` in
`features/controller/api/middleware.go` returns `true` when the caller tenant is `""`.

That intent is correct for a genuine mTLS admin. The defect is that a deliberate root
admin and a plumbing bug are indistinguishable: any path that reads the wrong context
key, forgets to propagate the tenant, or uses `context.Background()` instead of the
request context arrives at the same `""` and is granted unrestricted cross-tenant
access with no error and no log line.

A survey of `features/controller/api` on `origin/develop` found 195 HTTP handlers that
read a caller-supplied identifier, of which 101 never read the caller's tenant at all;
about 77 of those sit behind `requirePermission`, so an authenticated caller reaches
them. The scope helper is correct and is simply not called — 22 of 133 handler files
call it.

Because the default is open, omission is the vulnerability. Adding call sites lowers the
count without removing the class; the next forgotten propagation reopens it.

## Desired State

Caller scope is an explicit value with three distinguishable states — root-scoped,
tenant-scoped, and unset — and unset denies. Only the authentication middleware can
produce the root-scoped state, and only from a verified admin certificate marker. A
handler cannot reach a store call carrying an unset scope. An architecture test fails
the build when a handler reads a caller-supplied identifier without consuming that
value, so the remaining call-site work becomes enumerable and verifiable rather than
hand-audited.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] A scope type in `pkg/ctxkeys` (or a package it may import) represents exactly three
      states: root-scoped, tenant-scoped with a path, and unset. The unset state is the
      zero value.
- [ ] Only the authentication middleware constructs the root-scoped state, and only from a
      verified admin certificate marker. No other package can construct it.
- [ ] A helper that answers "may this caller act on this resource tenant" returns false for
      the unset state, and logs the denial with the route and the reason.
- [ ] `isWithinTenantScope` keeps its existing correct subtree semantics, including the
      trailing-separator guard that prevents `root/msp-a` matching `root/msp-ab`.
- [ ] A Go architecture test, following the pattern of `TestNoRawLeaderPrimitiveOutsidePkgHA`
      in `pkg/ha/architecture_test.go`, fails when a handler in `features/controller/api`
      reads a caller-supplied identifier and does not consume the scope value.
- [ ] The architecture test detects a handler whose route is registered through a wrapper
      indirection, not only one registered directly. A survey found 21 handlers registered
      that way, including 8 in `handlers_workflows.go`.
- [ ] A handler that is legitimately pre-authentication carries an explicit annotation with
      a written reason, in the style of `//architecture:allow-raw-leader`. There is no
      exemption list and no broadened exclusion path.
- [ ] `RegisterWorkflowRoutes` fails closed: a nil permission-gate dependency is a startup
      error, not a silently ungated route.
- [ ] `make check-architecture` runs the new test and fails on a violation.
- [ ] Tests cover the unset state denying, the root state allowing, a tenant state allowing

message_tool_only: stranded-reply recovery re-prompts the model to publish its private final and force-sends an English error notice to the DM (no config to disable)

## Summary

In `message_tool_only` mode (`messages.visibleReplies: "message_tool"`), a turn that ends with a **private** final text and no `message(action=send)` is classified as a "stranded reply". The recovery then:

1. **re-prompts the model with the private text verbatim** and tells it to deliver it: *"Your previous reply was not delivered … Your reply text was: "<finalText>" … Please deliver this reply now by calling message(action=send). Do not add any extra commentary; just deliver the original reply."*
2. if the retry sends nothing, **delivers a runtime notice** to the chat — `I generated a reply but could not deliver it to this chat. Please try again.` — marked `isError` + `deliverDespiteSourceReplySuppression`, so no reply mode can hold it back.

This defeats the main reason to pick `message_tool` in a customer-facing DM: keeping the model's final text private. The code says `message_tool_only` "keeps normal final text private by design" (comment on `warnPrivateMessageToolFinal`), but recovery actively tries to publish that text, and there's no config key to turn it off.

## Environment

- OpenClaw **2026.9.6**, Linux, Telegram DM
- `messages.visibleReplies: "message_tool"`, `messages.groupChat.visibleReplies: "automatic"`
- Support agent answering end customers. Private finals are internal notes ("handled, nothing else to do; context: …"), and they can mention other conversations.

## Why we use `message_tool`

With the default `automatic` mode, the agent answered the customer via `message(action=send)` and then wrote an internal note as its final text. That note went out as a second Telegram message about 3 s later. We saw 8 such leaks in about 10 turns. Switching to `message_tool` fixed that: `final reply suppressed by sourceReplyDeliveryMode: message_tool_only … deliverDespiteSuppression=false` shows up in the debug log exactly as expected.

1. Send a DM that makes the model end a turn with a long (≥280 chars) final text and no `message` call. In our case this was a duplicate of an already-answered request, and the model wrote itself a 937-char note summarising what it had done.
2. Gateway log: `final reply suppressed by sourceReplyDeliveryMode: message_tool_only … textChars=937 deliverDespiteSuppression=false`. This part is correct.
3. Right after that, `resolveStrandedReplyRecovery` returns `kind: "retry"`. A follow-up run is injected with the prompt above, which contains the full private note, and with `toolsAllow: ["message"]`.
4. Our model **refused**, because the note referenced other customers' cases. A more compliant model would have sent the internal note to the customer. That is the leak `message_tool` is supposed to prevent.
5. The retry sent nothing, so `kind: "diagnostic"` delivered `I generated a reply but could not deliver it to this chat. Please try again.` to the customer DM, in English, although the conversation was in Polish.

Our current workaround is prompt discipline: "if you did not send, end the turn with exactly `NO_REPLY`". Because `isSilentReplyText` makes the classifier return `none`, this avoids both the retry and the notice. Compose: config set MYSQL_PASSWORD breaks the instance; no way to rotate the database password

On Compose, there is no supported way to rotate the bundled database's root password, and the obvious attempt breaks the wiki.

`canasta config set MYSQL_PASSWORD=<new>` updates `.env` (and `vars.yaml` on gitops instances), then restarts. But the `db` service only reads `MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=${MYSQL_PASSWORD}` when it initializes an empty data directory. On an existing volume, the account in MariaDB keeps the old password, so after the restart:

- the web container can no longer connect to the database
- the `db` healthcheck (`mariadb-admin ping -u root -p$MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD`) fails

K8s already blocks this key in `config set` and prints a rotation procedure (`roles/config/tasks/_validate_key.yml`). Compose accepts it and silently produces a broken instance.

Rotating this credential is routine after any suspected exposure. For example, an RCE in a bundled extension (such as CVE-2026-100382 in ExternalData) exposes the web container's environment, which includes `MYSQL_PASSWORD`.

## Expected

On Compose with the bundled database (`USE_EXTERNAL_DB=false`), `config set MYSQL_PASSWORD=<new>` should:

1. Run `ALTER USER` for `root@'%'` and `root@'localhost'` in the running `db` container, authenticating with the current password and passing the new one outside argv and logs.
2. Only then write `.env` and `vars.yaml` and restart.

Alternatively, a dedicated command could do the same. Either way, `WIKI_DB_PASSWORD` needs the same handling when `--wikidbuser` is not root.

With an external database, `config set` should refuse, or warn that the password must be changed on the database server first.

ACH returns after settlement can't be recorded: late deposit returns cost the platform, late withdrawal returns strand customer money

## What happens

The ledger has no way to record an ACH return that arrives **after the entry settled**. `Services::Ach::Return` does only one thing: it calls `CancelStagedTransfer` on the real leg. That only works while the real leg is staged or pending. Once the entry settles, the leg is committed, Go answers `CancelStagedTransferRejected`, the service raises `Refused`, and nothing is recorded.

Real returns don't stop at settlement:
- Ordinary returns (R01 insufficient funds and the like) are due within 2 banking days of settlement.
- **Unauthorized-debit returns (R05, R07, R10) can arrive up to 60 days after settlement.**
- A withdrawal credit can also come back after it settles, for example when the receiving account is closed (R02).

## Why it matters

### A late deposit return is a loss to the platform, and first-party fraud exploits it

`ClearingPolicy` clears a deposit from the start of the 3rd Fed business day after it completed. Its comment says that's "until which an ACH return could still claw it back", which holds for ordinary returns but not for unauthorized ones. So an account owner can:

1. deposit $X by ACH debit from their own account;
2. wait for it to settle and clear (3 business days);
3. withdraw $X back to the same account, which is paid;
4. within 60 days, tell their bank the original debit was unauthorized (R10). The network takes $X back from the platform's bank.

The owner ends with the withdrawal and the refund. The platform is out $X, and **its ledger never learns**: the return can't be recorded, so the entity still looks square. The same money can also leave through another entity, via Securities (Purchase, then Draw to a colluding Borrower, then that Borrower's withdrawal). But a second party isn't needed.

The in-platform controls hold up to that point. Funding and every Securities money leg draw on *cleared* cash, and ruby ADR 0010 keeps an entity's cash covering its uncleared plus cleared cash, so uncleared money can't be spent or withdrawn. The exposure is entirely after clearing.

### A late withdrawal return is a loss to the customer

When a settled withdrawal credit is returned, the money comes back to the platform's bank, but the ledger can't re-credit the entity. Their money is stranded outside the ledger until someone reconciles by hand.

## What's needed (not yet designed)

- **Recording a post-settlement return.** For a deposit, reverse the settled real leg and its shadow leg, taking the money out of whichever of the entity's wallets still holds it. For a withdrawal, re-credit the entity.
- **What happens when the depositor no longer holds the money.** `cash` carries `debits_must_not_exceed_credits`, so today the ledger can't represent a customer who owes the platform. That needs a receivable, an overdraft allowance, or a recovery process.
- **An exposure policy for unauthorized returns**, which clearing doesn't cover. For example: hold or limit money leaving by ACH until 60 days, limits per entity or per deposit, or treating first deposits differently.

## Evidence

- `ruby/app/services/ach/return.rb`: returns only ever cancel the staged real leg.
- `ruby/app/services/ach/clearing_policy.rb`: `BUSINESS_DAYS = 3`, and the comment quoted above.
- `spec/alloy/ledger.als` now models a late return that the ledger can't see, with two checks, `UnclearedMoneyStaysBacked` and `LateReturnIsRecoverable`. They're running now, and their results will follow in a comment.

Authentication and the public demo mutations (`settleAch`, `clearAch`, ...) are out of scope here until deployment.

Carry pfSense conversion skips into F-1 findings, not just a report parameter

Filed from #302's review (@SamikaPerera). Not started -- this is the scope stub, deliberately kept out of #302 itself.

## The gap #302 does not close

#302 fixed the *disclosure* half of a real problem: a skip note from `pfsense_convert.py` (a rule it could not model) used to reach the user exactly once, at upload, and be gone by the time a report was downloaded later. That's fixed -- the downloaded report now carries the skip list and its coverage statement stops claiming "nothing was skipped" when something was.

It does not fix the *modelling* half. Skipping a `pass` rule makes the emitted Cisco ACL stricter than the real device. A policy rule asserting "this traffic must be denied" can then report `status="none"` (clean) against the emitted ACL, while the real firewall actually permits that traffic -- a genuine policy violation, reported as a pass. See `CLAUDE.md` section 7's "UPDATE, 6 September" entry for the full direction analysis (skipping a `block` rule is the safe, noisy direction; skipping a `pass` rule is the dangerous, silent one).

## The more complete fix

Carry each conversion skip into the F-1 findings list itself, as a `status="error"` card -- which is what it actually is: "part of this config could not be checked." That would:

- Show up on the dashboard directly, not only in a downloaded report.
- Be counted by `analysis/coverage.py` the same way any other blind spot is, rather than needing a second, parallel `conversion_gaps` parameter (which #302 added as the smaller, faster fix).
- Let a reader connect a specific skip to the specific policy rule it might be silently affecting, if the finding names the interface/rule clearly enough.

## Why this needs its own scoping, not a bolt-on to #302

- **Which check owns it?** A conversion skip isn't produced by `access_control`, `policy_compliance`, or `routing` -- it's a property of the source file, discovered before the pipeline ever runs a check. Needs an id prefix decision (not `PC-`/`AC-`/`RT-`/`CH-`/`CV-` -- another collision the team has cared about avoiding, most recently for #239's `cve_mapping`).
- **Where does it enter the pipeline?** `analysis/pfsense_convert.py`'s skip list is produced by `web/main.py`'s upload handler, before `analysis.pipeline.analyse()` is ever called. Getting it into the findings list means either widening `analyse()`'s signature (an F-3 shared-contract question) or injecting it after the fact in `web/main.py` the way `_attach_explanations()` already injects a key -- but a NEW finding is a bigger change than a new key on an existing one.
- **Does it apply beyond pfSense?** Today only `pfsense_convert.py` produces a skip list. If Cisco IOS parsing (via Batfish) can also silently drop something, the same mechanism should probably cover it too, which needs checking rather than assuming.

## Acceptance criteria (draft, not final -- needs a design pass first)

- [ ] Decide the id prefix and which module owns emitting these findings.
- [ ] Decide how the skip list reaches `analyse()`/the pipeline without widening `run(bf)`'s signature for every other check.
- [ ] A skipped rule appears as a `status="error"` finding on the dashboard, not only in a downloaded report.
- [ ] `analysis/coverage.py`'s `conversion_gaps` parameter (added in #302) is retired once this lands, since the findings list itself would carry the same information.
- [ ] Full suite green, mutation-tested the same as #302's own two guards.

[Bug]: Stale managed-update handoff lease from a dead triage run blocks all updates; update repair does not clear it (Windows, 2026.9.5)

### Summary
A `triage` action left a lease in `managed-update-handoffs.sqlite` with `phase: "uncertain"`. Both processes that owned it (executor and helper) had been dead for about two days, but every later `openclaw update` failed with:

```
Update recovery remains pending (update-failed). Retained state and artifacts were left for the owning updater to reconcile; automatic restart and repair were not attempted.
Another update executor owns this installation.
```

`openclaw update repair --yes` ran to completion (exit 0) but did not remove the lease, and the next `openclaw update` failed the same way. The only way out was deleting the row by hand.

### The stale row
`%LOCALAPPDATA%\Temp\openclaw\managed-update-handoffs.sqlite`, table `managed_update_handoffs` (1 row, last updated 2026-09-24 16:46 local):

```json
{
  "version": 2,
  "executor": { "pid": 33644, "startIdentity": "1790282395800" },
  "helper":   { "pid": 40680, "startIdentity": "1790281122000" },
  "action": {
    "kind": "triage",
    "phase": "uncertain",
    "lifetime": { "kind": "foreground",
                  "boot": { "platform": "win32", "identity": "2026-09-15T03:42:10.5000000Z" } }
  }
}
```

- Neither PID existed on 2026-09-26.
- The machine had not rebooted since 2026-09-15, so the boot identity still matched. My guess is that the stale check trusts "same boot" and never checks whether the PIDs are alive or match their `startIdentity`.

### Steps (as observed)
1. On 2026-09-24, a failed 9.4 → 9.5 hop led to an `openclaw triage` run that ended without releasing its lease (the processes are gone).
2. Two days later, with no reboot: `openclaw update --yes` (9.5 → 9.6) → "Another update executor owns this installation."
3. `openclaw update status --json` showed no active run.
4. `openclaw update repair --yes --json` → finalize steps completed, exit 0. The lease row was unchanged.
5. `openclaw update --yes` failed again with the same error.
6. I backed up the DB and deleted the row with `owner = '<uuid>'`. The next `openclaw update` got past admission and reached 2026.9.6.

### Expected
- A lease whose executor and helper PIDs are both dead (or whose `startIdentity` doesn't match) should count as stale even when the boot identity matches, **or**
- `openclaw update repair` (or `doctor --fix`) should detect and clear it, **or**
- the error should name the lease DB, the owner, and a supported command to release it.

### Related
#148454 / PR #148604 (self-conflict within a single managed upgrade) and #157157 (9.5 → 9.6 failure on macOS) look like different paths, as does #153401 (a live process owning `state-lifecycle`). Here the owner was a separate, dead `triage` run from two days earlier.

### Environment
Windows 11 Home, Node 24.18.0, npm global install (2026.9.5 at the time, updated to 2026.9.6 after clearing the row), gateway supervised by Windows Scheduled Tasks.

sec(ci): sibling deploy and sanity workflows grant id-token write to ungated jobs

Follow-up from LeanerCloud/cloud-commitments-cli#1649 / PR LeanerCloud/cloud-commitments-cli#1657. Same **structural** shape, but — unlike LeanerCloud/cloud-commitments-cli#1649 — no attacker-settable value reaches a `run:` block today, so this is hardening rather than a live vulnerability. Labelled accordingly.

## What

A structural sweep (parsing each workflow's YAML for `id-token` inheritance versus `environment:` bindings, rather than grepping) found jobs that hold `id-token: write` with **no** `environment:` binding:

| workflow | ungated jobs holding `id-token: write` |
|---|---|
| `deploy-aws-fargate.yml` | `prepare`, `test-deployment`, `summary` |
| `deploy-gcp.yml` | `prepare`, `build-and-deploy`, `test-deployment`, `summary` |
| `deploy-azure.yml` | `prepare`, `build-and-deploy`, `test-deployment`, `summary` |
| `aws_sanity.yml` | `sanity` |
| `azure_sanity.yml` | `sanity` |

All five declare `permissions: id-token: write` at **workflow** level, which hands it to every job whether or not that job authenticates.

Note `deploy-gcp.yml` and `deploy-azure.yml` are worse than `deploy-aws-lambda.yml` was: their `build-and-deploy` jobs actually assume cloud credentials *and* have no environment binding, so their OIDC subject is `repo:<org/repo>:ref:refs/heads/main` — the subject `terraform/environments/aws/ci-cd-permissions/role.tf:29` accepts unconditionally.

## Why this is not p0

The only untrusted value reaching a `run:` block in any of these is `inputs.environment`, and it is not injectable:

- on `workflow_dispatch` it is `type: choice` with options `[dev, staging, prod]`, which GitHub validates server-side;
- the `workflow_call` input is `type: string` (unvalidated), but the only caller is `deploy-all.yml`, whose own `environment` input is also `type: choice`.

So the escalation path exists structurally but has no injection to trigger it. `deploy-aws-lambda.yml` was the only one of the four with an attacker-settable value (`github.event.release.tag_name`) — that is LeanerCloud/cloud-commitments-cli#1649.

`github.actor` also reaches `run:` blocks in all four deploy workflows. GitHub usernames are `[A-Za-z0-9-]`, so those are **not** injectable; listed here only so a reader does not re-flag them.

## Fix

Apply the same split PR LeanerCloud/cloud-commitments-cli#1657 applied to `deploy-aws-lambda.yml`:

1. Remove `id-token: write` from workflow level; grant it per job, only to jobs that actually call `configure-aws-credentials` / `azure/login` / `google-github-actions/auth`.
2. Give those jobs an `environment:` binding so their OIDC subject is `environment:<name>` rather than `ref:refs/heads/main`.
3. Route `inputs.environment` through `env:` with a `dev|staging|prod` allowlist, since `workflow_call` types it as a free-form string.
4. Watch for the same reviewer trap LeanerCloud/cloud-commitments-cli#1649 had: `deploy-aws-fargate.yml`, `deploy-gcp.yml` and `deploy-azure.yml` all declare `outputs: environment: ...`, an output *named* environment that reads like a binding and gates nothing. PR LeanerCloud/cloud-commitments-cli#1657 renamed it to `target_environment`; do the same here.

Once all of these are gated, the `repo:<org/repo>:ref:refs/heads/main` subject can finally be dropped from the trust policy — currently it cannot, because these jobs plus `cleanup-staging.yml` and `destroy-fargate-dev.yml` (LeanerCloud/cloud-commitments-cli#1591) depend on it.

**Caveat:** per LeanerCloud/cloud-commitments-cli#1648, no Environment in this repo currently has protection rules, so an `environment:` binding buys the correct OIDC subject but not yet an approval gate. Steps 1-4 are still worth doing — they are the precondition for the gate to mean anything.

Related: LeanerCloud/cloud-commitments-cli#1649 / PR LeanerCloud/cloud-commitments-cli#1657, LeanerCloud/cloud-commitments-cli#1542 / PR LeanerCloud/cloud-commitments-cli#1641, LeanerCloud/

Hey HN! Tried to show this off a couple times before but didn't really get much traction, figured now that more time's been spent in the UI/UX side of things I'd give it another shot.

This is my attempt, started at the beginning of the year, to build a complete Magic: The Gathering engine.

Instead of coding individual card scripts, a compiler takes oracle text as input and outputs the card definition itself into executable effects that ran in the engine.

Another cool thing which is mentioned in the title is that tournaments can be played without relying on a central server hosting the game, and without having to trust in your opponents playing honestly. Shuffles carry a ZKP so that all peers can verify they were performed securely, and even complex cards like Praetor's Grasp which give you information about your opponent's cards that they themselves don't have work as expected with perfect secrecy!

I'd love to get some feedback on HN, especially regarding broken mechanics/scenarios and whatever potential improvements you think are worth adding.

Imagine giving ChatGPT or any other agent access to your Whatsapp/iMessage, bank transactions, health data, web pages you see, metadata about all the photos you took, places you visited, all your emails/documents, call logs, meeting notes, your voice mails, and more….

I built a context layer for that purpose. You can connect your Openclaw, Hermes, Claude, ChatGPT, Codex, etc to it. It gives your favorite agent "context superpowers". All the data is indexed and connected into a graph, self-hosted on your own hardware. Voice notes are transcribed, OCR runs on images in mails and pdfs, etc.

Omnesis offers a flexible data access model. For each agent you can define which source(s) they have access to and also guard data access with a privacy policy written in prose. You can also directly talk to the Omnesis agent which has no web search / internet tools — via a web portal or companion app — to ask the most intimate questions about your digital life.

I built this to be flexible. You can run all necessary models on zero-data-retention inference providers, or — if you can afford it — on your own hardware. I’ll keep investing in Omnesis’s security. Because it brings together sensitive data from many sources, please install it only on machines you control and keep secure.

The project also includes what I call “Omnesis Brain”. This is my work-in-progress take on what a “second brain” could look like on top of that context layer. Imagine an agent constantly analyzing your personal data in flux to maintain a more structured and grounded understanding of what’s happening in your life. This is experimental and disabled by default.

This has been a fun project to build over the last 6 months. Keen to answer questions!

[Bug] Unimplemented SSRF Protection in URL Controller allows internal network scanning

### Description
The `controller/url.js` file contains a detailed `validateURL` function designed to prevent Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) by checking if a URL points to a private/internal IP address. 

However, this function is **never called** anywhere in the application. Additionally, the required `dns` and `net` modules are not imported, so if it were called, it would crash. 

As a result, when a user creates a short link pointing to an internal IP (e.g., `http://169.254.169.254` or `http://127.0.0.1:27017`), the `fetchWebsiteTitle` function executes a server-side `fetch()` against the internal network. This constitutes a Blind SSRF vulnerability, allowing attackers to probe internal services and metadata endpoints.

### Steps to Reproduce
1. Submit a request to create a short URL pointing to `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/`.
2. Notice that the application does not reject the URL.
3. The server attempts to fetch the title of the page by making a direct request to the internal IP.

### Proposed Fix
1. Import the missing `dns` and `net` modules in `controller/url.js`.
2. Enforce the `await validateURL(url)` check inside `handleGenerateShortURL`, `handleGenerateShortUrlRender`, `handleUpdateShortURL`, and `handleBulkImport` before processing or saving the URL.
3. Add a fallback inside `fetchWebsiteTitle` to catch the rejection and fail safely.

Triage remaining code-scanning alerts on main

## Context
After #94 merged, the default branch has no open Dependabot alerts, but GitHub code scanning still reports 36 open alerts (checked 2026-09-28): 19 `cs/ecb-encryption`, 14 CredScan findings, and 3 `actions/missing-workflow-permissions`. The workflow-permission findings are addressed by #99. This issue tracks the remaining 33 alerts; the alert count alone does not establish 33 vulnerabilities.

## Preliminary source review
- All 19 ECB hits are `CipherMode.ECB` assignments in CFB, CCM, CMAC, OCB, SIV, OpenPGP, key-wrap implementations, or an OpenPGP test helper. These paths appear to use ECB as a single-block primitive; this does not yet prove the full encrypt/decrypt flows safe. No direct application plaintext ECB entry point was found in this source pass.
- Eight CredScan hits point to documentation, examples, or tests: sequential-byte Base64 in an XML example, sample passwords, and two PGP private-key test vectors attributed in source to OpenPGP.js. Six further hits are generated `bin`/`obj` XML copies of the XML example. The test-vector provenance and absence of live secrets still need confirmation before disposition.

## Review work
- Review each [ECB alert](https://github.com/KoalaFacts/HeroCrypt/security/code-scanning?query=is%3Aopen+rule%3Acs%2Fecb-encryption) against its full encrypt/decrypt flow. Confirm no caller exposes ECB as a mode for application plaintext. Record a code-level rationale for intentional primitive uses; fix any direct ECB encryption of user data. Start with [CFB #163](https://github.com/KoalaFacts/HeroCrypt/security/code-scanning/163).
- Review each CredScan finding against its source and provenance. Remove and rotate any real secret; otherwise scope the scanner or apply narrowly documented suppressions. Start with [test key #143](https://github.com/KoalaFacts/HeroCrypt/security/code-scanning/143) and [generated XML #159](https://github.com/KoalaFacts/HeroCrypt/security/code-scanning/159).
- Verify #99 closes workflow-permission alerts #104, #106, and #122 after it lands.

## Completion criteria
Every remaining alert has a verified disposition tied to code or fixture evidence. Any real vulnerability is fixed with focused tests; scanner exclusions or suppressions are limited to confirmed non-secret fixtures or required cryptographic primitives.

P1: Establish supply-chain security and deterministic toolchain governance

## Summary

Make dependency, action, runtime, package-manager, and container inputs explicit and continuously reviewed. Reduce avoidable toolchain ambiguity and add supply-chain controls appropriate for a public production site and future MDX compilation pipeline.

## Priority

**P1 — preventative security and reproducibility.** Begin after PR #51. Some cleanup can land with #52, but this issue owns policy and ongoing enforcement rather than repository formatting.

## Current state

Completed by #152:

- `flake.nix` / `flake.lock` own the development and CI toolchain;
- GitHub Actions owns required validation on minimal Dubnium JIT runners;
- Cloudflare Pages Functions / Wrangler own production runtime and deployment;
- GitLab is mirror-only and the divergent GitLab CI pipeline is removed;
- Docker is explicitly a secondary local portability path;
- Node 24, Yarn 1.22.22, Playwright 1.60.0, TypeScript 5.9.3, and Wrangler 4.114.0 authority is mechanically checked;
- frozen installs are enforced on CI/secondary install paths;
- stale scaffold metadata, drifting version claims, and mixed `npm run` indirection are resolved;
- build-only MDX/compiler content remains proven absent from request/browser runtime surfaces.

Still open:

- #157 adds immutable external Action pins, Dependency Review, and CodeQL; do not mark these complete until exact-head required CI is green and the PR merges;
- secret-scanning / push-protection posture still requires repository/organization settings evidence;
- dependency grouping/supersession remains shared-policy work in `hackelia-micrantha/.github#106`;
- artifact/SBOM scanning should be added only where an operational release artifact justifies a durable inventory/scanning contract.

## Goals

- Establish one documented and reproducible JavaScript toolchain.
- Detect vulnerable, malicious, stale, or unexpectedly expanded dependencies before merge.
- Keep CI actions and build inputs pinned and reviewable.
- Produce software inventory for deployed artifacts where useful.
- Clarify whether Docker is operational and scan it accordingly.
- Prevent build-only content tooling from entering runtime/browser dependency surfaces.

## Dependency and action controls

- Enable and configure Dependabot or Renovate with grouped, reviewable updates.
- Add pull-request dependency review and fail on defined severity/license/policy violations.
- Add CodeQL or equivalent first-party static analysis appropriate for TypeScript/JavaScript.
- Ensure secret scanning and push protection are enabled where repository/organization settings permit.
- Pin third-party GitHub Actions to immutable commit SHAs or document justified exceptions.
- Keep workflow permissions read-only by default and grant narrow job-level permissions only when required.
- Add lockfile integrity/frozen-install enforcement to all build and deployment paths.

## Runtime and package-manager normalization

- Select and document the supported Node major; align `engines`, CI, Docker, mise/tool-version files, and README.
- Define a deliberate TypeScript update policy and tested version.
- Keep Yarn as the package manager unless an explicit migration is approved.
- Remove unnecessary `npm run`/`npx` indirection from Yarn scripts.
- Decide whether `npm-run-all` remains justified or should be replaced with simpler task composition.
- Prefer a small `mise.toml` developer interface over overlapping Makefile/package/Docker wrappers where useful.
- Add `packageManager` metadata and Corepack policy if compatible with the chosen Yarn version.

## SBOM and artifact policy

- Generate an SBOM for deployed container images or release artifacts when those artifacts are operationally meaningful.
- Scan Docker images if Docker is retained as a production or parity artifact.
- Record whether the Cloudflare deployment artifact can be inventoried independently of Docker.
- Verify build-only MDX, validation

WGSL is_finite_value NaN/Inf guard is a float self-comparison that fast-math may fold away (activation.wgsl, relu.wgsl, bias.wgsl)

<!-- finding-id: SEC-e8e1dd84a447 -->
<!-- cwe: CWE-754 -->

Three WGSL kernels detect NaN / ±Inf with a float self-comparison helper,
`is_finite_value` (`value != value`, then `abs(value) <= MAX_F32`). WGSL does
not guarantee IEEE-754 NaN/Inf semantics at runtime — an implementation may
assume they are absent and an overflowing result is indeterminate, which is
why WGSL has no `isNan`/`isInf` builtin — so a backend compiling with
fast-math is free to fold both comparisons to "finite" and delete the guard.
Severity low (numeric integrity of discovery statistics only, no memory
safety impact: every index is still bounds-guarded), confidence low (reasoned
from the WGSL rules and wgpu-hal's Metal compile options, not reproduced on a
Metal device).

Found by the chunk 9 security sweep, Issue #2290 (shader layer #2232, tracker #2094).

## Why it matters

- `src/shaders/activation.wgsl:35` (`is_finite_value`), used at L210 (input
  skip) and L223 (the output guard that sets `valid = 1u`).
- `src/shaders/relu.wgsl:35`, used at L63 (input skip).
- `src/shaders/bias.wgsl:38`, used at L253, L264 and L273 — the only
  non-finite handling in that kernel (its `epsilon` uniform is never read).

Inputs are already filtered finite on the host
(`src/analysis/diagnostics/target_data.rs:74`–`:75`), so the guards that
matter are the *output* guards: a finite input can still overflow inside the
kernel — `incoming_weight * activation` (`activation.wgsl:216`–`:217`,
`bias.wgsl:261`), `gelu`'s `x * x * x` (`activation.wgsl:44`), and every
`x * x` square. When the guard is folded away, an Inf/NaN output is marked
`valid = 1u` and summed into the per-workgroup partial sums
(`activation_reduce.wgsl:44`–`:47`), so one overflowing sample poisons the
whole candidate's aggregate instead of being dropped as the CPU path drops
it. The host applies no finiteness check to the reduced sums in
`src/analysis/gpu/activation_evaluation.rs` (its two `is_finite` calls, L339
and L443, filter inputs only).

wgpu-hal 30's Metal backend builds shaders with a default `MTLCompileOptions`
(`wgpu-hal-30.0.1/src/metal/device.rs:272`) and never disables fast math,
which is Metal's default.

## Attacker model

A caller of the FFI analysis entry points who controls the recorded
activations / errors of a creature. FFI validation only requires them to be
finite (Issue #2135), so large finite values are accepted. No privilege
beyond submitting a discovery run.

## Trigger

A recorded activation (or `orientation * scale` / `incoming_weight`) large
enough that the kernel's product or square overflows f32 (|x| ≳ 1.8e19 for a
square, ≳ 7e12 for GELU's cube), analysed on a backend that compiles the WGSL
under fast-math (Metal by default).

## Exploit sketch

1. Submit training records where one sample's source activation is 1e20
   (finite, so FFI validation passes).
2. `activation.wgsl` computes `output_sq = output_val * output_val = +Inf`;
   the L223 guard, folded to `true`, marks it `valid = 1u`.
3. `activation_reduce.wgsl` adds `+Inf` into that workgroup's partial sum;
   the host totals it and the candidate's statistics become Inf/NaN, so the
   candidate is mis-scored (NaN never wins a `>` comparison; Inf can) instead
   of the single sample being skipped.

## Suggested fix

Replace the float self-comparison with an integer test that fast-math cannot
fold: `(bitcast<u32>(v) & 0x7f800000u) != 0x7f800000u` is `true` exactly for
finite `v`. Share it across `activation.wgsl`, `relu.wgsl` and `bias.wgsl`
(and `matching.wgsl` if it survives removal). Add a naga-validated CPU test
pinning the helper's body, and a GPU-gated test feeding an overflowing sample
that asserts `valid == 0`.

Spec: consolidate Worker readiness observations, authority, and admission

Part of #113.
Related implementation and review history: #118. Preserves the accepted contracts of #114, #115, and #116.

## Problem Statement

A Human operator needs Environment readiness to explain truthfully whether an Agent can work, without running a hidden model turn, exposing host credentials, or trusting an obsolete Worker connection. Today that guarantee depends on many callers performing the right validation and authority checks in the right order.

The repeated #118 reviews exposed the same invariant at successive interfaces: explicit probes, automatic probes, startup `worker/info`, enrollment observation methods, and the exposed readiness store. Individual repairs improved safety, but the system still distributes responsibility for trusted observations across transport, runtime orchestration, enrollment, persistence, presentation, and admission.

The current design also permits different interpretations of the same facts. Diagnostic execution against the current implementation demonstrated that an unknown target-model fact is considered available by Agent compatibility but refused by Agent-run admission. A second diagnostic demonstrated that a late older observation in the same Worker connection epoch replaces newer readiness, while the memory and SQLite adapters select different latest probe records. A Human can consequently receive inconsistent explanations even when individual validation tests pass.

This is a bounded consolidation of the readiness system, not another entry-point-specific patch and not permission to weaken strict admission.

## Solution

Give readiness one cohesive Module that owns the lifecycle of an Environment readiness probe observation: obtain current Worker authority, collect or accept the observation through that authority, validate and privacy-reduce it, determine its ordering and applicability, atomically record it, and return an identifiable committed result or an explicit refusal.

Startup, automatic, and Human-requested probes use that same processing contract. Current readiness and its probe metadata come from the same committed observation. Historical observations remain inspectable without acquiring current authority. Agent compatibility and admission share the same readiness evaluation, while health presentation continues to expose independent facts and decisive reasons.

The Human-visible result is consistent, explainable readiness across reconnects, configuration changes, concurrent probes, restart, and failed or malformed responses. Required unknown facts still block work. No new mechanism for proving account-level model entitlement is introduced by this consolidation.

## User Stories

1. As a Human operator, I want startup and explicitly requested probes to follow the same readiness rules, so that the reported result does not depend on how the probe was triggered.
2. As a Human operator, I want a probe request to return the observation that was actually committed, so that success corresponds to durable evidence.
3. As a Human operator, I want readiness details and their displayed probe metadata to identify the same observation, so that status and provenance cannot contradict one another.
4. As a Human operator, I want a late older probe to be unable to replace newer current facts, so that a slow response cannot make readiness regress to an obsolete observation.
5. As a Human operator, I want concurrent requests to have deterministic outcomes, so that their completion order does not silently change which observation is current.
6. As a Human operator, I want duplicate delivery of an observation to avoid duplicate history entries, so that retries do not fabricate additional evidence.
7. As a Human operator, I want malformed or incomplete Worker results to be refused before any durable mutation, so that partial evidence cannot establish readiness.

## Summary

After a board card's PR merges, the local base branch is advanced using a value taken directly from the PR's `baseRef` — a string controlled by whoever opened the PR on the forge. It is passed to `git pull` / `git fetch` with no validation and no `--` separator.

## Where

`apps/server/src/board/baseBranchSync.ts:76-89`:

```ts
const fastForward =
  currentBranch === baseBranch
    ? // Base is checked out here: pull it forward in the working tree.
      {
        operation: "board.pullMergedBaseBranch.pull",
        args: ["pull", "--ff-only", remoteName, baseBranch],
      }
    : // Base is not checked out: move its local ref straight from the remote
      // without a checkout. No leading `+` keeps it fast-forward-only.
      {
        operation: "board.pullMergedBaseBranch.fetch",
        args: ["fetch", remoteName, `${baseBranch}:${baseBranch}`],
      };
```

`baseBranch` comes from the forge — `apps/server/src/board/supervisorReactor.ts:4491-4493`:

```ts
const baseBranch = merged.pullRequest?.baseRef ?? null;
if (baseBranch !== null) {
  yield* pullMergedBaseBranch({ git, cwd: root, baseBranch }).pipe(
```

No shape check, no `check-ref-format`, no `--`.

## Why this one is worth fixing even though the sibling path is guarded

The **other** base-branch path — the card's configured `board.card.baseBranch` — *is* validated. `packages/contracts/src/board.ts:8960-8970` defines `isBoardCardBaseBranchShape`, which rejects empty, untrimmed, whitespace, `refs/`-prefixed, `origin/`-prefixed, leading/trailing `/`, and `..`. It is enforced on both write paths, `apps/server/src/board/decider.ts:862` (create) and `:1383` (update), via `validateBaseBranch` at `:455-466`.

So the codebase already knows this class of input needs a shape check. The gap is that `pullMergedBaseBranch` — reached on the *merge* path, from forge data rather than user data — does not use it. That asymmetry is the actual bug: the same conceptual input, validated on one path and not the other.

## Reproduction

1. Open a PR against a repository the board is configured to watch, with `baseRef` set to a hostile value such as `--upload-pack=touch /tmp/pwn` or another git option.
2. Merge it.
3. The board's merge reactor advances the local base and reaches `git pull --ff-only <remote> --upload-pack=...` (if base is checked out) or `git fetch <remote> <base>:<base>` (if not).
4. Git parses the value as an option rather than a refname.

Practical exploitability depends on the forge: a `baseRef` reaching this code has already been through the forge's own PR validation, and the git argv is not a shell, so the blast radius is "git options", not arbitrary shell. The concrete risk is an unvalidated string from an external party reaching a command that mutates the **root checkout's** ref state — and the fast-forward-only intent, which is what protects the root checkout here, is not the thing standing between it and damage.

`isBoardCardBaseBranchShape` permits a **leading dash**. `"-upload-pack=x"` passes every predicate.

# Project Charter: Detección de intrusiones en redes con Machine Learning

## 1. Resumen

La idea del proyecto es armar un sistema de detección de intrusiones (NIDS) basado en Machine Learning. El sistema recibe los datos de un flujo de red (protocolo, servicio, duración, bytes y paquetes enviados en cada sentido, TTL, etc.) y decide si ese flujo es tráfico normal o un ataque. Como segunda tarea, también intentamos predecir de qué tipo de ataque se trata.

Para esto usamos el dataset UNSW-NB15 con la división en train y test que publicaron sus autores. Vamos a comparar una regla simple sin IA y una regresión logística contra XGBoost, validar con cross-validation sobre el train y evaluar el modelo final una sola vez sobre el test. Al final queremos tener un pipeline reproducible y un script de consola que reciba un CSV con flujos y devuelva las predicciones.

## 2. Definición del problema

Los IDS tradicionales funcionan con firmas, es decir, reglas escritas a mano para ataques ya conocidos, y les cuesta detectar variantes nuevas. Nuestra propuesta es entrenar un modelo que aprenda cómo se comporta el tráfico malicioso a partir de ejemplos etiquetados, para que funcione como una capa más de detección.

Planteamos dos tareas sobre los mismos datos:

- **Binaria (tarea principal):** normal o ataque.
- **Multiclase (tarea secundaria):** Normal o una de las 9 categorías de ataque del dataset (Analysis, Backdoor, DoS, Exploits, Fuzzers, Generic, Reconnaissance, Shellcode y Worms).

### PEAS

| | |
|---|---|
| Performance | Tarea binaria: recall de ataques y tasa de falsos positivos, además de F1 y PR-AUC. Tarea multiclase: Macro-F1 y F1 por clase. |
| Environment | Registros de flujos de red del dataset UNSW-NB15. Es un entorno parcialmente observable porque solo tenemos los metadatos del flujo y no el contenido de los paquetes. Es estático, ya que trabajamos sobre archivos CSV. |
| Actuators | Para cada flujo, el sistema devuelve una etiqueta (normal/ataque o categoría de ataque) junto con su probabilidad. |
| Sensors | Las 42 variables que trae cada registro: protocolo, servicio, estado de la conexión, duración, bytes y paquetes por sentido, TTL, pérdidas, jitter, tiempos del handshake TCP, tamaño medio de los paquetes y contadores de conexiones recientes. |

## 3. Datos

Usamos UNSW-NB15, un dataset armado por el Australian Centre for Cyber Security de UNSW Canberra (Moustafa y Slay, 2015). Lo descargamos desde la página oficial (research.unsw.edu.au/projects/unsw-nb15-dataset). Trabajamos solamente con la partición en train y test que publicaron los autores:

- `UNSW_NB15_training-set.csv`: 175.341 registros.
- `UNSW_NB15_testing-set.csv`: 82.332 registros.

Cada registro tiene 45 columnas. De esas, 42 son las variables que usamos como entrada (39 numéricas y 3 categóricas: `proto`, `service` y `state`). Las otras tres son `id`, que es un índice de fila y se descarta, y las dos etiquetas: `label` (0 = normal, 1 = ataque) y `attack_cat` (la categoría del ataque, o "Normal").

También existe una copia del dataset en Kaggle, pero ahí los archivos de train y test tienen los nombres cambiados. Por eso usamos la versión oficial y verificamos los archivos con su hash MD5 antes de entrenar. Los hashes y los pasos para descargar los datos están en `data/README.md`.

## Outcome
A deliberately broken parser rule is corrected and re-deployed to a test device within the sync schedule, with no app release, and tampered-payload rejection is demonstrated in the same rehearsal.

## Context
**Risk R6 (parser rot) is a certainty, not a possibility.** Banks change SMS formats without notice,
per bank and per template. If fixing a broken parser requires an app release plus store review plus
user update adoption, we are permanently weeks behind reality — and the failure is invisible: the
app simply stops seeing some transactions.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Parser rules expressed as versioned data (patterns + field mappings), not compiled code
- [ ] The app fetches and caches an updated rule set on a schedule
- [ ] New rules apply **without an app release**, verified end to end
- [ ] Rule sets are signed or integrity-checked; a tampered rule set is rejected
- [ ] Safe rollback: a bad rule set can be reverted centrally
- [ ] Bundled default rules ship with the app so a fresh install works offline
- [ ] Rule evaluation is sandboxed — a malformed rule cannot crash the app
- [ ] Per-sender parse-success telemetry, with alerting on degradation

## Technical notes
- The telemetry is as important as the mechanism: without per-sender success rates, parser rot is
  discovered by user complaints, which means trust is already lost.
- Integrity-check the rule payload. Remotely delivered parsing logic that an attacker could
  substitute would be a serious vulnerability.
- Version the rule-set payload schema (patterns, field mappings, signature, version number) so the app can reject a payload whose schema_version it does not recognise, rather than attempting to parse it.
- Publish the signing-key rotation contract: how a new signing key is introduced without invalidating rule sets already cached on devices mid-rotation.

## Test notes
- Break a parser deliberately, push a corrected rule set, confirm recovery with no app update.
- Serve a tampered payload → rejected.
- Serve a malformed rule → app remains stable, falls back to bundled rules.
- Signature-rotation test: a device holding a rule set signed by the outgoing key still validates correctly during a key rotation window, without a gap in trusted parsing.
- Sandbox-escape negative test: a deliberately malicious rule payload attempting excessive resource use or a malformed regex is contained without affecting other app functions.

## Security and privacy
- Treat an unsigned or badly signed rule payload as a spoof-risk equivalent to a spoofed SMS sender: reject it, do not fall back to partial trust, and alert on repeated rejection from the same fetch endpoint.
- Confirm the remote-config fetch itself carries no user data beyond what is strictly needed to select the correct rule set, so the update channel does not become a privacy leak.

## Observability
- Alert when per-sender parse-success telemetry drops below a defined threshold for any bank sender, distinct from simply collecting the telemetry.
- Track rule-set fetch failures and stale-cache duration per device cohort, so a broken distribution path is caught before it silently degrades parsing for weeks.

## Rollout and rollback
- Stage a new rule set to a small device cohort and compare its parse-success telemetry against the prior rule set before promoting it to all devices.
- Rehearse the safe-rollback path on a schedule, not only when something breaks, so the mechanism is proven working before it is needed under pressure.

Bug: Event editor, calendar and check-in page hide the server's reason when an action fails

**Pre-submission checks**
- [x] I searched existing issues and did not find a duplicate.
- [x] This is not a security vulnerability.

**What happened?**
When the events API refuses an action it says why, but the event editor, the calendar's event modal and the check-in page drop that reason. They show a generic toast ending in "Please try again", or nothing at all. Trying again cannot succeed while the reason stands. Same class of bug as #10126 (groups area).

Found by trying to delete an event with someone checked in. `DELETE /api/events/{id}` answers:

```json
{"success":false,"message":"Cannot delete event: 1 people are currently checked in.","error":"Cannot delete event: 1 people are currently checked in.","code":409}
```

but both delete buttons show only **"Failed to delete event. Please try again."** The other 409, `Cannot delete event: event is currently assigned to a kiosk.`, is dropped the same way.

All reproduced in the browser (admin). "Elsewhere" means a second tab changed the record while the page stayed open.

| Page | Action | Server said | Toast |
|------|--------|-------------|-------|
| Event editor (`/event/editor/{id}`) | Delete Event, one person checked in | 409 `Cannot delete event: 1 people are currently checked in.` | "Failed to delete event. Please try again." |
| Calendar (`/event/calendars`), event modal | Delete, same event | same 409 | "Failed to delete event. Please try again." |
| Event editor | Save, event deleted elsewhere | 404 `Event not found` | "Failed to save event. Please try again." |
| Check-in page (`/event/checkin/{id}`) | Check In All, event deactivated elsewhere | 409 `Cannot check in to an inactive event. Activate the event first.` | "Check-in failed. Please try again." |
| Check-in page | Check Out All, event deleted elsewhere | 404 `Event not found` | "Check-out failed. Please try again." |
| Check-in page, group roster | a person's Check In / Check Out button, event deactivated elsewhere | 409, same reason | nothing; the button is re-enabled |
| Check-in page | Delete attendance record, record already deleted elsewhere | 404 `Not found.` | "Failed to delete. Please try again." |

Not affected (already show the server's `message`): walk-in Check In and the single Check Out on the check-in page, family check-in on Family View, and the event list's delete (it uses `window.CRM.APIRequest`).

Code:
- `webpack/event-form.js`: `saveEvent()` and `deleteEvent()` reject with `new Error(\`HTTP ${r.status}\`)` and never read the body. Their callers in `webpack/event-editor.js` and `webpack/calendar-event-editor.js` then show fixed strings.
- `webpack/event-checkin.js`: `#checkinAllBtn`, `#checkoutAllBtn` and `deleteAttendanceRecord()` throw `HTTP ${status}` and show fixed strings. The `.roster-action-btn` handler only re-enables the button.

**What did you expect to happen?**
The toast shows the server's reason, e.g. "Cannot delete event: 1 people are currently checked in.", so the user knows to check people out, deactivate the event or free the kiosk first. The existing translated message is kept for network errors and non-JSON responses.

**Steps to reproduce**
1. Log in as admin. Create a group with one member, then create today's event for it (e.g. Sunday School class page → **Create Today's Event**, or `POST /api/events/quick-create` with the group id).
2. On `/event/checkin/{id}`, check the member in.
3. Open `/event/editor/{id}` → **Delete Event** → **Delete**. `DELETE /api/events/{id}` → 409 with the reason above; the toast says "Failed to delete event. Please try again." Same from the calendar: click the event → **Delete** → **Delete**.
4. Back on `/event/checkin/{id}`, deactivate the event from another tab (event list → Deactivate, or `POST /api/events/{id}/status` with `{"active": false}`). Then click **Check In All**: 409 `Cannot check in to an inactive event. Activate the event first.

datasets pinned <4.0 blocks fix for CVE-2026-66007 (path traversal), same in 0.17.0

garak's dependency spec pins `datasets>=3.0.0,<4.0` (both `pyproject.toml` and `requirements.txt`). This is unchanged in the current latest release, 0.17.0.

This range is entirely inside the vulnerable range for **CVE-2026-66007** — a path traversal (CWE-22) in `datasets`' folder-based dataset builders, where an unsanitized `file_name` metadata field lets a crafted dataset read arbitrary local files via directory traversal, exposed when `save_to_disk()`/`push_to_hub()` is called on the loaded dataset. Fixed upstream in `datasets` 5.0.1 (advisory: PYSEC-2026-3716).

Because garak caps `datasets<4.0`, downstream consumers can't pick up the fix without breaking garak's own install:

```
pip install --dry-run garak==0.17.0 datasets==5.0.1
# ResolutionImpossible: garak 0.17.0 depends on datasets<4.0,>=3.0.0
```

Could the `datasets` ceiling be raised/tested against `>=5.0.1`?

ajv (Another JSON Schema Validator) before 8.18.0 is vulnerable to Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS) when the $data option is enabled. The pattern keyword accepts runtime data via JSON Pointer syntax ($data reference), which is passed directly to the JavaScript RegExp() constructor without validation. An attacker can inject a malicious regex pattern (e.g., "^(a|a)*$") combined with crafted input to cause catastrophic backtracking. A 31-character payload causes approximately 44 seconds of CPU blocking, with each additional character doubling execution time. This enables complete denial of service with a single HTTP request against any API using ajv with $data: true for dynamic schema validation. This issue is also fixed in version 6.14.0.
